summary: The day lends itself to three checkable tasks on plain Python lists and dicts (ELT's raw stage beside its clean table, rejects with a reason and a load-log dict, an append behind a watermark) and one SQL statement with a named @ parameter; its BigQuery DDL, connections, pandas and google-cloud-bigquery job, pytest and review steps need a cloud project, packages or a test runner, or teach a concept a check cannot see.

steps.title: ETL and ELT: where the transform runs
steps.reason: The page's three-function job on lists makes where the transform runs visible: in ELT the staging list keeps every raw row and the clean list is built from it, while the source list is left unchanged. Filtering before the stage (ETL by mistake) or removing bad rows from the source both leave lists a check can read.

steps.title: The steps of a pipeline: stage, validate, log
steps.reason: The rejects-with-a-reason loop and the load-log dict are plain Python whose results a check reads, and the page names the silent drop and the counts that must add up. A sibling with a second row rule stays off the 06 rung, which does the same split in pandas.

steps.title: Reruns and incremental loads
steps.reason: The watermark on lists is runnable as shown: max(..., default=0), a comprehension above the watermark and an append, and a second call that adds nothing is the idempotence the page teaches. Leaving out default=0 raises on the first run and appending without the watermark doubles every row, both page-named.

steps.title: External data, connections and transfers
steps.reason: External tables, EXTERNAL_QUERY, connections, Sheet exports and the Data Transfer Service exist only in BigQuery and the console; SQLite has none of them, and a view standing in for an external table would fake the point of the step.

steps.title: Parameterized queries
steps.reason: Python's sqlite3 binds an @kind placeholder from a dict the way BigQuery does (confirmed under CPython 3.15; the browser pass is the proof for Pyodide), so one SQL statement can be run with two values and an injection string. A literal pasted in place of @kind, or @kind written inside quotes, gives rows a check can tell apart; the bq --parameter flag itself stays out, since it is typed at a shell.

steps.title: Building the ETL job
steps.reason: The step's code is pandas (merge, duplicated, isin, assign) and google-cloud-bigquery load jobs, none of which the runtime has. A standard-library rewrite of the sort-then-drop-duplicates rule would need sorting with a key, which the page does not teach, and it is the 06-etl-job clean_events rung itself.

steps.title: Testing the transforms with pytest
steps.reason: The step teaches pytest, fixtures and a module split across files: a tool and a layout, with no pytest and only one file in the runtime.

steps.title: Review: the week as one pipeline
steps.reason: The review retells the week's pipeline and compares architectures (ETL warehouse, ELT warehouse, lake): concepts and trade-offs with no behaviour a check can see.

tasks.title: ETL and ELT
tasks.idea: The reader writes elt(source, staging, clean), the ELT order on lists: it copies every source row into staging unchanged, then appends to clean only the staged rows whose kind is in EVENT_KINDS = ("open", "assigned", "closed"). Called with source = [{"event_id": 1, "kind": "open"}, {"event_id": 2, "kind": "closd"}] and two empty lists, staging ends with both rows and clean with only event 1.
checks: staging holds every source row, the misspelt closd row included; filtering before the stage, as an ETL job does, leaves it out.
clean holds only the rows whose kind is one of the three, built from staging after the load.
source still holds all of its rows after the call; removing bad rows from the source breaks the rule that extract reads without changing it.
tasks.q: EVENT_KINDS holds the three kinds an event may have. Write elt(source, staging, clean), which runs the ELT order on three lists of event dicts. First it copies every row of source into staging unchanged, bad rows included. Then it appends to clean each row of staging whose "kind" is in EVENT_KINDS. It fills the two lists it is given and leaves source holding all of its rows. Called with source = [{"event_id": 1, "kind": "open"}, {"event_id": 2, "kind": "closd"}] and two empty lists, staging ends with both rows and clean with only event 1.
tasks.tests:
source = [{"event_id": 1, "kind": "open"}, {"event_id": 2, "kind": "closd"}, {"event_id": 3, "kind": "closed"}]
staging, clean = [], []
elt(source, staging, clean)
assert staging == [{"event_id": 1, "kind": "open"}, {"event_id": 2, "kind": "closd"}, {"event_id": 3, "kind": "closed"}], "staging holds every source row, the misspelt closd row included"
assert clean == [{"event_id": 1, "kind": "open"}, {"event_id": 3, "kind": "closed"}], "clean holds only the staged rows whose kind is in EVENT_KINDS"
assert source == [{"event_id": 1, "kind": "open"}, {"event_id": 2, "kind": "closd"}, {"event_id": 3, "kind": "closed"}], "source still holds all of its rows after the call"

tasks.title: Rejects and the load log
tasks.idea: The reader writes validate(rows) returning (clean, rejects, log). A row whose kind is not in EVENT_KINDS is rejected with reason "unknown kind", and a row whose ticket_id is None with reason "no ticket"; log is {"rows_read": ..., "rows_loaded": ..., "rows_rejected": ...}. For one good row, one closd row and one row with ticket_id None, rejects carries two rows with their reasons and log is {"rows_read": 3, "rows_loaded": 1, "rows_rejected": 2}.
checks: Each bad row appears in rejects with every source key plus its reason; dropping it silently leaves rejects empty.
The ticket_id None row carries "no ticket" and the closd row "unknown kind", so each reject says why.
log's rows_loaded plus rows_rejected equals rows_read, with all three counts right.
The dicts in the input list carry no reason key afterwards; writing row["reason"] in place changes the source rows, where {**row, "reason": ...} builds a new dict.
tasks.q: Write validate(rows), which checks a list of event dicts and returns three things: clean, rejects, log. A row whose "kind" is not in EVENT_KINDS is rejected with the reason "unknown kind", a row whose "ticket_id" is None is rejected with the reason "no ticket", and every other row goes to clean. Each reject is a new dict holding all of the row's keys plus "reason", in the order the rows came, and the dicts in rows are left with no "reason" key. log is {"rows_read": ..., "rows_loaded": ..., "rows_rejected": ...} with the three counts. For one good row, one row of kind "closd" and one row whose "ticket_id" is None, rejects holds the two bad rows with their reasons and log is {"rows_read": 3, "rows_loaded": 1, "rows_rejected": 2}.
tasks.tests:
rows = [
    {"event_id": 12, "ticket_id": 2, "kind": "closed"},
    {"event_id": 13, "ticket_id": 2, "kind": "closd"},
    {"event_id": 14, "ticket_id": None, "kind": "open"},
]
clean, rejects, log = validate(rows)
assert [clean, [{k: v for k, v in r.items() if k != "reason"} for r in rejects]] == [[{"event_id": 12, "ticket_id": 2, "kind": "closed"}], [{"event_id": 13, "ticket_id": 2, "kind": "closd"}, {"event_id": 14, "ticket_id": None, "kind": "open"}]], "clean keeps the good row, and each bad row is in rejects with every one of its own keys"
assert [r.get("reason") for r in rejects] == ["unknown kind", "no ticket"], "each reject carries the reason for the rule it broke"
assert log == {"rows_read": 3, "rows_loaded": 1, "rows_rejected": 2}, "log counts the rows read, loaded and rejected, and loaded plus rejected equals read"
assert ["reason" in r for r in rows] == [False, False, False], "the dicts in rows gain no reason key"

tasks.title: Incremental loads
tasks.idea: The reader writes append_new(source, staged), an append load behind a watermark on event dicts: it reads the highest event_id in staged (0 when staged is empty), appends to staged every source event above it, and returns the list of new events. With source events 1 to 5 and staged holding 1 to 3, it appends and returns events 4 and 5; a second call returns [] and leaves staged at five rows.
checks: On an empty staged list it loads every source event; max without default=0 raises ValueError on that first run.
With 1 to 3 staged it appends only events 4 and 5, not event 3 again; a >= comparison duplicates the watermark row.
A second call returns [] and staged still holds five events, so the append is safe to repeat; appending the whole source each run doubles every row.
tasks.q: Each event is a dict with an "event_id". source is the list of events the source holds now, and staged the list of events already loaded. Write append_new(source, staged), an append load behind a watermark. It reads the watermark, the highest "event_id" in staged, or 0 when staged is empty. It appends to the list staged itself every source event whose "event_id" is above the watermark, and returns the list of those new events. With source events 1 to 5 and events 1 to 3 staged, it appends and returns events 4 and 5; a second call returns [] and leaves staged at five events.
tasks.tests:
source = [{"event_id": n, "kind": "open"} for n in [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]]
first = []
assert [e["event_id"] for e in append_new(source, first)] == [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], "on an empty staged list, the first run loads every source event"
staged = source[:3]
new = append_new(source, staged)
assert [[e["event_id"] for e in new], [e["event_id"] for e in staged]] == [[4, 5], [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]], "with events 1 to 3 staged, it returns and appends only events 4 and 5"
again = append_new(source, staged)
assert [again, len(staged)] == [[], 5], "a second call returns [] and staged still holds five events"

tasks.title: Parameterized queries
tasks.idea: The reader writes one SQL statement in QUERY that counts the events of one kind per ticket from a fact_ticket_events table, with the kind as the named parameter @kind: columns ticket_id and events, most events first. The checks run the same QUERY with {"kind": "closed"}, then {"kind": "open"}, then a value carrying a quote and OR 1=1.
checks: Run with kind closed, QUERY returns the closed counts per ticket, most first; writing '@kind' inside quotes compares against the text @kind and returns nothing.
Run again with kind open, the same QUERY returns the open counts; a statement with 'closed' pasted in place of @kind returns the closed rows both times.
Run with the value x' OR '1'='1, QUERY returns no rows, because a bound value is compared as a string and never becomes part of the WHERE clause.
tasks.q: The checks build a fact_ticket_events table with the columns event_id, ticket_id and kind, one row per ticket event. Write one SQL statement that counts the events of one kind for each ticket, with the kind given as the named parameter @kind. It returns two columns, ticket_id and events (the count), one row per ticket that has events of that kind, most events first. Type the statement between the triple quotes. The checks run the same QUERY three times, with the kind closed, then open, then the value x' OR '1'='1. Run with closed it returns (4, 2) then (2, 1); run with the third value it returns no rows.
tasks.starter:
QUERY = """
-- events of one kind per ticket, most first
"""
tasks.tests:
import sqlite3
conn = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
conn.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE fact_ticket_events (
    event_id INT,
    ticket_id INT,
    kind VARCHAR(10)
);
INSERT INTO fact_ticket_events (event_id, ticket_id, kind)
VALUES (1, 2, 'open'), (2, 2, 'closed'),
       (3, 4, 'open'), (4, 4, 'closed'), (5, 4, 'open'), (6, 4, 'closed'),
       (7, 6, 'open'), (8, 6, 'assigned'), (9, 6, 'open'), (10, 6, 'assigned'), (11, 6, 'open');
""")
cur = conn.execute(QUERY, {"kind": "closed"})
closed_rows = [[c[0] for c in cur.description], cur.fetchall()]
assert closed_rows == [["ticket_id", "events"], [(4, 2), (2, 1)]], "run with kind closed, it returns ticket_id and events, the closed counts per ticket, most first"
open_rows = conn.execute(QUERY, {"kind": "open"}).fetchall()
assert open_rows == [(6, 3), (4, 2), (2, 1)], "run again with kind open, the same QUERY returns the open counts"
injected = conn.execute(QUERY, {"kind": "x' OR '1'='1"}).fetchall()
assert injected == [], "run with the value x' OR '1'='1, it returns no rows"
